_meta: iter 86 → iter 87: curated idiom pairs for 🔀 Swap-Bench drill. Each entry pairs two JS snippets and asks 'same observable behavior?'. Forces transfer-of-mental-model — recognizing that two different syntactic idioms reach the same result (or that two near-identical-looking idioms diverge). Iter 86 shipped at 12 pairs; iter 87 expanded to 18 (Map vs object, parseInt radix trap, sort in-place vs immutable, `==` vs `===`, async/await vs .then chaining, JSON parse depth). Each snippet capped at 8 lines for mobile-stacked readability. Mix of same/different roughly 50/50.

pairs.title: Doubling an array
pairs.explain: map() returns a NEW array; the for-loop MUTATES the original. Different observable effect on `arr`.

pairs.title: Keep positive numbers
pairs.b:
const out = arr.reduce((acc, x) =>
  x > 0 ? [...acc, x] : acc, []);
pairs.explain: Both produce a new array of positive numbers in original order. reduce-with-accumulator is a hand-rolled filter.

pairs.title: Loop over array elements
pairs.explain: for-of yields VALUES; for-in yields KEYS (indices as strings). for-in on arrays is the classic JS trap — also walks inherited enumerable props.

pairs.title: Merge two arrays
pairs.explain: Both produce a new shallow-merged array, original arrays untouched. Behavior is identical for plain arrays.

pairs.title: Iterate object properties
pairs.explain: Object.keys returns OWN enumerable string keys; for-in walks own AND inherited enumerable keys. Different on objects with a custom prototype.

pairs.title: Create a 3-row matrix of empty arrays
pairs.explain: Array.from with a factory calls the function PER row → 3 independent arrays. Array(3).fill([]) puts the SAME array reference in every slot — pushing to grid[0] also mutates grid[1] and grid[2].

pairs.title: Default value when null/undefined
pairs.a:
const out = x !== null && x !== undefined
  ? x : fallback;
pairs.explain: Nullish coalescing `??` is exactly the explicit null/undefined check. Different from `||` (which also triggers on 0, '', false).

pairs.title: Default value for x = 0
pairs.explain: `||` triggers on every falsy value (0, '', false, NaN, null, undefined). `??` triggers ONLY on null and undefined. For x = 0, `||` returns fallback; `??` returns 0.

pairs.title: Get the first 3 elements
pairs.explain: slice() returns a NEW array, `arr` unchanged. splice() REMOVES the first 3 from `arr` and returns them. Same return for the first call only — `arr` is now shorter.

pairs.title: Dedupe an array
pairs.b:
const out = arr.filter((x, i) =>
  arr.indexOf(x) === i);
pairs.explain: Both keep the FIRST occurrence of each value in original order. Set version is O(n); filter+indexOf is O(n²).

pairs.title: Shallow-clone an object
pairs.explain: Both produce a new object with the same own enumerable string-keyed properties. Both are SHALLOW (nested objects share references).

pairs.title: Sum 1..n
pairs.explain: Both return the same total. The recursive version eats stack frames (no TCO in JS engines) — same result, different cost profile.

pairs.title: Use a number as a lookup key
pairs.explain: Both return 'a' here — but only because `1` survives the object's string-key coercion (`o['1']`). Map preserves the original key TYPE (so `m.get('1')` would return undefined); plain object stringifies all keys.

pairs.title: Convert '08' to a number
pairs.explain: Both return 8. Modern engines no longer treat leading-0 as octal in parseInt (ES5+). The classic trap was '08' → 0 in older engines; today both forms agree. Different on '08px' though — parseInt returns 8, Number returns NaN.

pairs.title: Sort an array ascending
pairs.a:
arr.sort((a, b) => a - b);
return arr;
pairs.explain: sort() MUTATES `arr` in place and returns the same reference. toSorted() (ES2023) returns a NEW array, leaving `arr` untouched. Different observable effect on `arr` between calls.

pairs.title: Compare 0 to false
pairs.explain: `==` performs type coercion: `false` becomes `0`, so `0 == false` is true. `===` requires same type AND value: number vs boolean → false. Classic interview trap.

pairs.title: Read then transform
pairs.explain: Both return a Promise that resolves to the parsed JSON. The async version is syntactic sugar — `await` unwraps the promise, then the return value is auto-wrapped. Identical observable result and error-propagation behavior.

pairs.title: Clone a deeply-nested object
pairs.explain: Spread is SHALLOW — nested objects share references. JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...)) is DEEP for plain data (loses functions, undefined, Symbols, Dates → strings, but recurses through nested objects). After mutating obj.nested.x, only the spread clone reflects the change.
